meta.title: Who really said "Do not go where the path may lead, go instead where there is no path and leave a trail"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Robert Frost and not Emerson. The line traces to Muriel Strode’s 1903 poem in The Open Court — and her original wording was different.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Do not go where the path may lead, go instead where there is no path and leave a trail'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Robert Frost and not Emerson. Muriel Strode wrote it in The Open Court, August 1903 — as a vow, not a command.

answer.label: Not Robert Frost — Muriel Strode, reworded
answer.sourceLine: Robert Frost is one of several famous names this line gets pinned to, and Quote Investigator ↗, whose chronology documents no source for any of them, traces the saying instead to a page of aphorisms by the American poet Muriel Strode printed in the Chicago journal The Open Court in August 1903. Strode wrote it as a vow in the first person — “I will not follow where the path may lead…” — and the familiar imperative wording is a later, unascribed rewrite.

source.excerpt:
I will not follow where the path may lead, but I will go where there is no path, and I will leave a trail.

Infinitely will I trust nature’s instincts and promptings, but I will not call my own perversions nature.

Each receives but that which is his own returning.
Each hears but that which is the echo of his own call.
Each feels but that which has eaten into his own heart.
trail: August 1903 — the first strong match. Muriel Strode’s “Wind-Wafted Wild Flowers” appears in The Open Court, opening with the line in the first person. Read the scanned issue ↗.

The specialist verdict. Quote Investigator ↗ tentatively credits Strode with originating the statement, notes that Fred V. Hawley spoke a different version a month later, and concludes that the Emerson linkage — and by extension the other famous credits — is not substantive.

1983 to 1992 — the rewrite takes hold. The modern imperative wording turns up unascribed in a 1983 yearbook; the first Emerson credit Quote Investigator has found is a January 1992 Middle School Journal caption. Barry Popik’s entry ↗ reaches the same conclusion about Emerson.
Still circulating under the wrong name. Goodreads carries the imperative version credited to Emerson ↗, while poetry-quote sites print it credited to Robert Frost ↗.

source.useLine: Strode’s 1903 wording is public domain — free to use, including in commercial and paid presentations, with no permission or licence needed. The later imperative rewrite is not her wording and has no identified author, so nothing here establishes who, if anyone, holds rights in that phrasing.
source.rightsNote: The source we cite and quote — The Open Court, Volume 17, Number 8, August 1903 — was published in the United States long before 1931, so Muriel Strode’s original text is in the public domain. One honest caveat: the familiar imperative rewrite is not Strode’s wording and no author for it has ever been identified, so nothing here establishes who, if anyone, holds rights in that later phrasing.

author.name: Muriel Strode
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: Muriel Strode was born in Bernadotte Township, Illinois, in 1875 and married Samuel David Lieberman in 1908, but published throughout under her birth name. Her books include My Little Book of Prayer (copyright 1904), My Little Book of Life (1912), A Soul’s Faring (1921) and At the Roots of Grasses (1923). She has no Wikipedia entry and very little surviving biography — and the one sentence of hers that everyone knows travels under other people’s names.

cite.sourceCitation: Muriel Strode, “Wind-Wafted Wild Flowers,” The Open Court 17, no. 8 (August 1903): 505. The popular imperative wording is a later rewrite; the earliest instance of this exact wording in Quote Investigator’s chronology is a January 1992 Middle School Journal caption, while a close variant (“Do not follow where the path may lead…”) appears without ascription in a 1983 University of Michigan Medical School yearbook.

misattribution.heading: Two famous names, neither of them right
misattribution.intro: This saying attracts big names the way a magnet attracts filings. Quote Investigator’s inquiry opens by listing the people it gets pinned on — Emerson, George Eliot, Robert Frost, George Bernard Shaw — and its chronology documents no source for any of them; the verdict it states outright, that the linkage is “not substantive,” is about Emerson.

items.why: Quote sites still print “Do not follow where the path may lead… Go instead where there is no path and leave a trail” over Frost’s name — here is one doing it ↗. Quote Investigator ↗ names Frost among the occasional credits and documents no source for the attribution; the line was already in print in 1903, under Muriel Strode’s name.

Quote Investigator quotes the reference author Ralph Keyes on the Emerson claim — no source for it has ever been found in Emerson’s works — and concurs that the linkage is not substantive. The earliest Emerson credit QI has located is a caption in Middle School Journal in January 1992, many years after his death ↗. Barry Popik ↗ reaches the same conclusion.

items.scope: The poem it gets confused with
items.why: Frost’s two-roads poem was first published in the August 1915 Atlantic Monthly and opened Mountain Interval in 1916 ↗. It is about a choice between two existing roads and contains no line about making a path or leaving a trail — but it is very likely why Frost’s name gets attached here at all.

At the American Osteopathic Association’s 1905 annual meeting a four-line sung version was credited to Still, the founder of osteopathy, as Quote Investigator records ↗. That was after Strode’s poem was already in print, and after the Rev. Fred V. Hawley had sung a near-identical version at a Unitarian conference in September 1903.

misattribution.truthLine: The trail leads to Muriel Strode, “Wind-Wafted Wild Flowers,” The Open Court, August 1903 ↗ — and Quote Investigator credits her only tentatively, leaving room for future research to find something earlier.

context.heading: How a vow became a command
lead: The sentence people put on graduation cards is a rewrite of something quieter. In August 1903 the Chicago journal The Open Court printed a page of aphorisms called “Wind-Wafted Wild Flowers” by Muriel Strode, and the first of them ran: “I will not follow where the path may lead, but I will go where there is no path, and I will leave a trail.” It is a vow the speaker makes about herself, not an instruction issued to anyone else.

Somewhere between the journal and the poster shop the vow turned into a command. Quote Investigator’s chronology ↗ finds the modern imperative wording in print with no ascription at all in a 1983 medical-school yearbook, and the first credit to Ralph Waldo Emerson — the name it usually carries today — in a January 1992 issue of Middle School Journal. Robert Frost picks up the overflow, an easy slip given that his best-known poem is about choosing between two roads.
context.detailsSummary: The line’s early travels, before anyone said “Emerson”
detailsBody: September 1903. At a national conference of Unitarian churches in Atlantic City, the Rev. Fred V. Hawley quoted a sung four-line version — “I need not follow the beaten path; / I do not hunt for any path; / I will go where there is no path, / And leave a trail” — a month after Strode’s poem appeared, per Quote Investigator ↗.

August 1905. The same four-line version was spoken at the American Osteopathic Association’s annual meeting in Colorado and there credited to Andrew Taylor Still, the founder of osteopathy, according to Quote Investigator’s chronology. Strode’s own line was reprinted in My Little Book of Prayer (copyright 1904) and, credited to her by name, in the New York State Journal of Medicine in July 1906.

1984 and after. A United Press International profile of the country singer Bill Anderson described a picture above his desk carrying a shortened form of the saying; by September 1992 a Pennsylvania middle school had hung the modern wording on a new sign above its office in foot-high red cursive letters, with Emerson’s name attached.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator lists Robert Frost, George Eliot and George Bernard Shaw among the occasional credits, quotes Ralph Keyes that no source for the Emerson attribution has ever been found in his works, gives Muriel Strode's August 1903 poem in The Open Court (vol. 17, no. 8, p. 505) as the earliest strong match, records Fred V. Hawley's September 1903 sung version, the 1905 Andrew Taylor Still credit, the 1983 unascribed yearbook instance, the 1984 Bill Anderson UPI item, and the January 1992 Middle School Journal caption as the earliest Emerson credit, and tentatively credits Strode.

The August 1903 issue of The Open Court (Vol. 17, Iss. 567) contains, in its Miscellaneous section, 'WIND-WAFTED WILD FLOWERS. BY MURIEL STRODE.' opening 'I will not follow where the path may lead, but I will go where there is no path, and I will leave a trail.' followed by 'Infinitely will I trust nature's instincts and promptings...' and 'Each receives but that which is his own returning...'
Barry Popik's entry gives the August 1903 Open Court vol. 17 no. 8 p. 505 citation for Strode's line and states the saying is often incorrectly credited to Ralph Waldo Emerson, who never wrote it.
Southern Illinois University's OpenSIUC carries the catalogue record for Muriel Strode's 'Wind-Wafted Flowers' in The Open Court, Vol. 1903, Iss. 8, Article 5, with a recommended citation.

Muriel Strode was born 16 February 1875 in Bernadotte Township, Illinois and died 25 January 1964; she married Samuel David Lieberman in 1908; her books are My Little Book of Prayer (1904), My Little Book of Life (1912), A Soul's Faring (1921) and At the Roots of Grasses (1923); her 1903 line became misattributed to Ralph Waldo Emerson beginning around the 1990s.
Robert Frost's 'The Road Not Taken' was first published in the August 1915 issue of The Atlantic Monthly and then as the opening poem of the 1916 collection Mountain Interval.

This page prints 'Do not follow where the path may lead... Go instead where there is no path and leave a trail.' under the heading 'Quote by Robert Frost', showing the Frost misattribution in live circulation.
Goodreads displays 'Do not go where the path may lead, go instead where there is no path and leave a trail.' credited to Ralph Waldo Emerson.
